about.title: About Temperature Converter
description: This temperature converter is designed for everyday and technical work where a value needs to move cleanly between Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin, and Rankine.

It is useful for weather checks, cooking adjustments, lab notes, equipment documentation, and any workflow where the wrong scale can make a result look correct at first glance but still be interpreted incorrectly.

howTo.title: How to Use the Temperature Converter

steps.title: Enter the source temperature
steps.description: Start with the exact temperature value you have, including negative values if needed.

steps.title: Choose the original scale
steps.description: Select the scale the number currently belongs to, such as Celsius for weather data or Fahrenheit for a recipe written for a US audience.

steps.title: Select the target scale
steps.description: Choose the format you actually need for the next step in your workflow, such as Kelvin for a science context or Fahrenheit for a kitchen display.

steps.title: Check whether the result is physically reasonable
steps.description: Use quick intuition checks, such as water freezing around 0°C or 32°F, to catch obvious scale mix-ups.

tips: Negative values are common in Celsius and Fahrenheit, but Kelvin cannot go below absolute zero.
Cooking, weather, and lab contexts often use different default scales.
If the converted result looks suspicious, check whether you selected the wrong input scale rather than assuming the formula is wrong.

faq.q: When should I use Celsius, Fahrenheit, or Kelvin?
faq.a: Celsius is common for weather and international everyday use, Fahrenheit is common in the United States for daily life and cooking, and Kelvin is standard in scientific and engineering contexts where absolute temperature matters.
No. Kelvin starts at absolute zero. If you see a negative Kelvin result, the input scale or value has been handled incorrectly.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to catch a scale mistake?
faq.a: Compare against known anchors. Water freezes at 0°C and 32°F, and boils at 100°C and 212°F under standard conditions. If the result disagrees with those anchors in an obvious case, recheck the selected scale.

faq.q: Why does the same weather report look very different in another unit?
faq.a: Because the scales use different zero points and increments. A normal outdoor temperature can look small in Celsius and much larger in Fahrenheit without meaning anything has changed physically.

faq.q: Is this tool suitable for science and engineering work?
faq.a: It is useful for quick conversion and checking, but important technical work should still be validated against the source specification, instrument, or calculation workflow you are using.

faq.q: What is the most common temperature conversion mistake?
faq.a: Selecting the wrong input scale is more common than the formula itself being wrong. That mistake can produce a number that looks reasonable but belongs to the wrong context.
